Magic of sacred geometry

Sacred geometry is the study of shapes and proportions, such as the circle, the spiral and the star, that appear in nature, art and architecture. Many traditions treat them as symbols of unity, balance and growth.

Drawn with a compass and a ruler

Most sacred geometry shapes start with a compass and a ruler.

Keep the compass set to one width. Draw a circle, move the needle to any point on its edge, and draw a second circle. The two circles make the Vesica Piscis, and repeating that single step builds the Seed of Life and the Flower of Life. The straight lines of Metatron’s Cube need only a ruler.

Vesica Piscis

Two circles of the same size, each passing through the other’s centre.

The almond-shaped lens where they overlap is the starting point for most of the patterns below. Its width to height ratio is 1 to √3.

Meaning

Union of opposites and the birth of new possibilities.

When you draw it

Drawing the Vesica Piscis begins with the simplest movement: two circles meeting. While the hand guides the compass, attention gathers and breathing settles. In symbolic work, this shape helps you see how two sides, such as desire and action, or you and another, can overlap and create a new space, and notice that your idea is born in that overlap.

Fibonacci spiral

Squares of side 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and 21, joined by quarter-circle arcs.

Each number is the sum of the two before it. The ratio between neighbours settles near 1.618, the golden ratio, which is why the same spiral shows up in shells, seed heads and galaxies.

Meaning

Growth, natural rhythms, and the unfolding of life.

When you draw it

The Fibonacci spiral is drawn gradually, square by square, arc by arc. This rhythm teaches patience and attention to the process, not only the result. In symbolic work, the spiral helps you feel growth step by step: to see what your path is made of, and to ask which small next step grows naturally from the ones before.

Seed of Life

Seven circles: one in the centre and six around it.

Each new circle is centred on a point where two earlier circles cross. It is the first stage of the Flower of Life and a common shape for a quiet moment of focus.

Meaning

Creation, new beginnings, and infinite potential.

When you draw it

The Seed of Life is drawn from a single point: one circle, then another, six times around the centre. It is a simple, repeating practice that helps you return to the centre and slow down. In symbolic work, the seed is a reminder of beginnings, a good shape for reflecting on what you want to plant now: a new habit, a project or an intention.

Merkaba

Two tetrahedra locked together, one pointing up and one down.

Geometers call it the star tetrahedron. The outlined octahedron in the centre is where the two shapes meet. Contemplative traditions read the pair as two opposites held in balance: above and below, giving and receiving.

Meaning

Unity of body, mind, and spirit; protection and expanded awareness.

When you draw it

Drawing the Merkaba joins two triangles, one pointing up and one down. Careful, focused line work helps you feel the balance between opposites. In symbolic work, the Merkaba is a reminder of balance, between action and rest, giving and receiving, and helps you notice which side of your life needs more attention now.

Flower of Life

Overlapping circles of one size on a hexagonal grid, framed by a ring.

Keep adding circles in the same way and the pattern repeats without end. Many traditions use it as an image to rest the eyes on while breathing slowly.

Meaning

Interconnectedness, unity, and the unfolding of creation.

When you draw it

The Flower of Life is built from identical circles repeated again and again. The steady, rhythmic movement of the hand is calming and helps you let go of extra thoughts. In symbolic work, the flower shows that everything is connected: each circle rests on its neighbours. While drawing it, you can reflect on your relationships, on support, and on where you feel part of a whole.

Metatron’s Cube

Thirteen circles joined by 78 straight lines.

The circles come from the Fruit of Life. Joining every centre to every other draws a cube, a star and hidden outlines of all five Platonic solids.

Meaning

Balance, cosmic order, and the connection between all forms.

When you draw it

Metatron’s Cube asks for precision: thirteen circles and many straight lines joining their centres. This work trains attention and patience. In symbolic work, the cube helps you see order behind complexity: how many different connections add up to one pattern. While drawing it you can put your thoughts in order and ask what in your life needs to be connected or clarified.

Torus

A ring-shaped surface with flow running up through the centre, over the top, down the sides and back in underneath.

Switch between the 3D form and the 2D view from above, drawn as tilted circles that wind around the ring. The same pattern appears in the field around a magnet, and it is a popular symbol for continuous flow.

Meaning

Continuous energy flow, renewal, and balanced giving and receiving.

When you draw it

Drawing a torus on paper is a meditative practice in which the lines become a symbol of the continuous flow of energy. By repeating smooth movements, we slow down, gather our attention and explore where we feel stuck and where we are ready for change. In symbolic work, the torus helps you picture energy moving where things once felt still, and turn your attention to your intention: to clarify an idea or give momentum to a new project.

Sri Yantra

Nine interlocking triangles surrounded by lotus petals and a square gate.

Four triangles point upward and five point downward, meeting at a central point called the bindu. Traditionally, the upward triangles are linked with the masculine and the downward ones with the feminine.

Meaning

Harmony of masculine and feminine; a journey toward inner stillness.

When you draw it

Drawing the Sri Yantra is a slow, exacting practice. Each triangle has to meet the others at precise points, so the mind has to stay with the pen. Many people use it as a path inward: starting at the outer square and moving toward the central point, they let attention settle with each line. In symbolic work, the central point is a place to rest and ask what you want to hear in stillness.

Tree of Life

Ten circles joined by twenty-two paths.

In the Kabbalistic tradition the circles, called sephirot, are stages through which the divine becomes the world, and the paths show how they connect.

Meaning

Connection between the divine, creation, and the human soul.

When you draw it

Drawing the Tree of Life means placing ten points and then connecting them one path at a time. The process is a way to slow down and trace how things relate. In symbolic work, you can place yourself on the tree: ask which circle you are in now, and which path leads to the next stage.

Platonic Solids

Five three-dimensional forms whose faces are all identical regular shapes.

The tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, icosahedron and dodecahedron are the only solids built from identical regular faces meeting in the same way at every corner. Plato linked four of them to fire, earth, air and water, and the fifth to the cosmos.

Meaning

Five geometric forms traditionally linked to the elements and cosmic harmony.

When you draw it

Drawing solids in perspective asks you to look closely at edges, corners and depth. Moving from one form to the next gives the practice a natural rhythm. In symbolic work, each solid can stand for an element, so you can pause and ask which element you need more of now: the warmth of fire, the steadiness of earth, the lightness of air or the flow of water.

Fruit of Life

Thirteen circles of the same size: one in the centre, six around it, and six more beyond.

It grows out of the Seed of Life and the Flower of Life, and joining the centres of its circles with straight lines draws Metatron’s Cube.

Meaning

A pattern of 13 circles symbolising creation and underlying geometric order.

When you draw it

The Fruit of Life is drawn circle by circle, each one touching its neighbours. The repetition is calming and gives the hand and eye something steady to follow. In symbolic work, it invites you to think about what has grown from your earlier steps, and what you are ready to harvest or share.

Pentagram

A five-pointed star drawn in one continuous line.

Each line crosses two others at points that divide it in the golden ratio, so the pentagram is full of the same proportion that appears in the Fibonacci spiral.

Meaning

Traditionally associated with protection, harmony, and the five elements.

When you draw it

The pentagram is drawn in a single continuous line, which makes it a practice in flow and focus. Many people draw it slowly, one point at a time. In symbolic work, the five points can stand for five elements or five areas of life, such as body, mind, work, relationships and rest, a simple way to check where you feel balanced and where you need more care.
